chunks.title: Age-related cataract types
chunks.tldr: Nuclear = yellow-brown, myopic shift ('second sight'). Cortical = spokes/wedges, glare. PSC = glare, worse reading and in bright light.
points: Posterior subcapsular (PSC): granular plaque in front of the back capsule. Black and vacuolated on retroillumination (Wedl/bladder cells). At the nodal point → big effect on vision. Glare from headlights, worse with a small pupil (reading, sunlight).
Anterior subcapsular: fibrous metaplasia of lens epithelium.
Nuclear sclerosis: exaggerated ageing. Yellow → brown → (rarely) black. ↑ refractive index → myopic shift → can read without glasses again ('second sight of the aged').
Cortical: clefts → wedge/spoke opacities, often start inferonasally. Glare.
Christmas tree: colourful needle-like crystals (also in myotonic dystrophy).
Maturity: immature (partly opaque) → mature (fully opaque) → hypermature (shrunken, wrinkled capsule) → Morgagnian (cortex liquefies, nucleus sinks).
chunks.hook: Nuclear = Near-sighted shift. PSC = Problems with Pupil small (reading, bright light).

cards.q: Which cataract causes 'second sight of the aged'?
Cataract where liquefied cortex lets the nucleus sink?

chunks.title: Cataract from disease, drugs & injury
chunks.tldr: Learn the shapes: snowflake (diabetes), stellate/Christmas tree (myotonic dystrophy), shield (atopic), glaukomflecken (past acute angle closure), flower/rosette (blunt trauma).
points: Diabetes: glucose → sorbitol → lens swells. Refraction swings (high sugar → myopic). Rare young snowflake cataract. Age-related cataract earlier.
Myotonic dystrophy (90%): iridescent 'Christmas tree' → stellate PSC.
Atopic dermatitis (~10%): shield-like anterior subcapsular plaque, young, both eyes.
NF2: early PSC/capsular cataract (>60%).
Chronic anterior uveitis: commonest secondary cataract (+ steroids). Starts as a polychromatic sheen at the posterior pole.
Glaukomflecken: grey-white anterior subcapsular flecks = infarcts from a past acute angle closure (pathognomonic).
High myopia, RP, LCA, gyrate atrophy, Stickler → PSC.
Steroids → PSC. Chlorpromazine → anterior stellate.
Trauma = commonest one-sided cataract in the young. Blunt → flower-shaped. Electric shock → milky/snowflake. Infrared (glassblowers) → true capsular exfoliation. Radiation → PSC (delayed).
chunks.hook: Glaukomflecken = a fossil from an old angle-closure attack.

cards.q: Grey-white anterior subcapsular flecks in the pupil area?
cards.a: Glaukomflecken: sign of previous acute angle closure.

cards.q: Shield-like anterior subcapsular cataract in a young adult with eczema?
True exfoliation of the anterior capsule occurs in?

chunks.title: Pre-op checks for cataract surgery
chunks.tldr: Ask about tamsulosin (floppy iris), anticoagulants (check INR), allergies (iodine, latex). Examine for: RAPD (cataract never causes it), lid disease, guttata, shallow AC, small pupil, PXF.
points: Indications: visual (daily life affected) or medical (phacolytic/phacomorphic glaucoma, need to see/treat the fundus).
General: control diabetes/BP, wait 3–6 months after MI, 6 months after stroke, can they lie flat?
Drugs: alpha-blockers (tamsulosin) → IFIS. Antiplatelets usually continued. Warfarin: INR in range, check within 24 h.
Allergies: iodine (use chlorhexidine), latex, hyaluronidase (insect-bite cross-reaction).
Eye: cover test (amblyopia, squint), RAPD = posterior pathology, treat blepharitis/dacryocystitis/ectropion first (endophthalmitis risk).
Cornea: guttata → protect endothelium. AC depth, pupil dilation, red reflex (trypan blue if poor).
Lens: hard brown/black nucleus (consider ECCE). PXF → weak zonules, phacodonesis, small pupil.
Fundus: AMD etc. Dense cataract → B-scan for RD. Long/thin eyes or buckles → avoid peribulbar block.
chunks.hook: Tamsulosin = Trampoline iris (floppy).

cards.q: Drug most associated with intraoperative floppy iris syndrome?
Patient with cataract has an RAPD. What does it mean?
cards.a: Additional posterior pathology (retina/optic nerve): cataract never causes an RAPD.

chunks.title: Consent: risk numbers to know
chunks.tldr: Key numbers: PC rupture ~1%, dropped nucleus ~0.2%, RD <1%, endophthalmitis ~0.1% (1 in 1000), suprachoroidal haemorrhage ~0.04%. Severe sight loss ~1 in 1000.
points: Most operations are straightforward with good results.
~1 in 1000 left with little/no sight. ~1 in 10,000 lose the eye.
Common, mild: bruising, drop allergy, IOP spike, iritis, PCO.
Less common: PC rupture/vitreous loss ≤1%, zonular dehiscence, dropped nucleus ~0.2%, wound leak, CMO, corneal decompensation, refractive surprise, RD <1%, IOL dislocation, ptosis, diplopia.
Rare but serious: endophthalmitis 0.1%, suprachoroidal haemorrhage 0.04%.
Anaesthesia risks (blocks): retrobulbar haemorrhage, globe perforation, brainstem anaesthesia.
Other eye: essentially no risk (sympathetic ophthalmia extremely rare).
chunks.hook: 1 in 100 capsule breaks. 1 in 1000 gets infected.

cards.q: Approximate risk of endophthalmitis after cataract surgery?
Approximate risk of suprachoroidal haemorrhage?

chunks.title: Biometry & choosing the target
chunks.tldr: IOL power needs keratometry + axial length. Optical biometry is best. Special care for short eyes (Hoffer Q) and post-refractive surgery eyes (Haigis-L etc.). Aim for slight myopia (~−0.25 D).
points: Optical (partial coherence interferometry): non-contact, accurate, also measures K, ACD, white-to-white.
A-scan ultrasound: contact or (better) immersion. For dense cataracts.
Formulae: SRK/T, Haigis, Hoffer Q, Holladay 1 & 2. Hoffer Q often for short eyes. Short eyes = most surprises.
After LASIK/PRK: standard formulae fail (overestimate corneal power → hyperopic surprise). Use history method, CL method, Masket, Haigis-L. Warn the patient.
Stop soft CLs ~1 week, rigid 2 weeks before biometry.
Personalised A-constant corrects a surgeon's consistent error.
Target: emmetropia or slight myopia (−0.25 D). Hyperopia tolerated worse.
Keep within ~2 D of the other eye (aniseikonia), unless that eye will be done soon.
Monovision: non-dominant eye −1 to −2 D. Multifocal IOLs: need accurate refraction, may cause glare.
Under ~55: warn about losing accommodation with a monofocal IOL.
chunks.hook: K + AL = IOL. Previous LASIK? Special formula, warn about surprises.

cards.q: Two measurements needed for basic IOL calculation?
Max usual refractive difference between the two eyes to avoid aniseikonia?

chunks.title: IOLs: where they go & what they're made of
chunks.tldr: Best place = in the bag. Torn capsule → 3-piece IOL in the sulcus (never a 1-piece) or an AC lens. Square edges reduce PCO. Toric IOLs can rotate.
points: IOL = optic + haptics.
Positions: bag (ideal), sulcus (3-piece only), AC (angle-supported, special lens). Add-on sulcus lens for refractive surprise (avoid in very short eyes → angle closure).
Hydrophobic acrylic: thin, but more dysphotopsia.
Hydrophilic acrylic (hydrogel): biocompatible, but past problems with calcification, more PCO.
Silicone: biocompatible, but silicone oil sticks to it (avoid in oil-filled eyes).
PMMA: rigid, 5–6 mm incision, cheap (developing countries), more PCO.
Square-edged optic → less PCO (but more dysphotopsia).
Blue-light filters, aspheric optics (better contrast), heparin coating (uveitis, unproven).
Toric: for corneal astigmatism; can rotate → reposition early.
Multifocal/bifocal, 'accommodating', light-adjustable IOLs.
chunks.hook: Capsule torn? 3 pieces in the sulcus, never 1.

cards.q: Which IOL design feature reduces posterior capsular opacification?
Why avoid silicone IOLs in eyes with silicone oil?
cards.a: Silicone oil deposits on the IOL.

chunks.title: Anaesthesia & manual cataract surgery
chunks.tldr: Mostly local: sub-Tenon (safe), peribulbar (good akinesia, rare globe perforation), topical. ECCE = big incision, nucleus out whole. MSICS = self-sealing scleral tunnel, cheap and fast.
points: GA: children, young adults, anxiety, learning difficulties, dementia, tremor, epilepsy.
Sub-Tenon: blunt cannula inferonasally 5 mm from the limbus. Good analgesia, variable akinesia, chemosis/subconj haemorrhage.
Peribulbar: 25 mm needle. Good akinesia. Globe perforation risk → avoid in long eyes.
Topical ± intracameral lidocaine: no akinesia, fewer anaesthetic complications, slightly more surgical ones.
ICCE (old): cryoprobe removes lens + capsule.
ECCE: big capsulotomy, 8–10 mm limbal incision, nucleus expressed whole, sutures (astigmatism).
MSICS: sclerocorneal tunnel, stained capsule, nucleus out manually. As good as phaco, faster, no expensive machine.
chunks.hook: Long eye → no sharp needle (use sub-Tenon or topical).

cards.q: Why avoid peribulbar blocks in high myopes?
cards.a: Higher risk of globe perforation (long eye, thin sclera).

cards.q: What is MSICS?
cards.a: Manual small-incision cataract surgery via a self-sealing scleral tunnel.

chunks.title: Phaco machine settings & viscoelastics
chunks.tldr: Bottle height = AC pressure. Flow (AFR) = how fast things come to the tip. Vacuum = how tight it grips. Surge after occlusion breaks = capsule danger. Cohesive OVD makes space; dispersive coats the endothelium.
points: Higher AFR → need a higher bottle. Trainees: keep AFR and vacuum low.
Post-occlusion surge: when the blockage breaks, a sudden rush out → AC collapses → capsule rupture risk.
Peristaltic pump: vacuum builds only when the tip is occluded.
Venturi pump: vacuum always available, flow tied to vacuum.
Phaco tip: titanium needle vibrating ultrasonically, cooling sleeve protects the wound. Torsional modes use less energy.
Cohesive OVD (e.g. Healon GV): fills/maintains space (capsulorhexis, IOL insertion), pushes the iris back, easy to remove, bigger IOP spike if left.
Dispersive OVD (e.g. Viscoat): coats and protects the endothelium, plugs small capsule tears, harder to remove, traps bubbles.
Soft shell: dispersive under cohesive, for guttata.
chunks.hook: Cohesive = Creates space. Dispersive = Defends the endothelium.

cards.q: Which OVD type is better for protecting the endothelium?
Which pump generates vacuum only when the tip is occluded?

chunks.title: Phaco step by step
chunks.tldr: Povidone-iodine 5% (3 min) → drape lashes → side port + main incision → capsulorhexis → hydrodissection → divide & conquer / chop → cortex aspiration → IOL in the bag → intracameral antibiotic.
points: Povidone-iodine 5% in the fornix and on the lids, wait ≥3 minutes. Drape out the lashes.
Side port ~60° from the main incision. Main incision on the steep axis or temporal (less astigmatism, maybe slightly more endophthalmitis).
Continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis (cystotome/forceps). Poor red reflex → trypan blue.
Hydrodissection: fluid under the capsule edge → frees the nucleus (see the fluid wave).
Divide & conquer: sculpt a cross, crack into quarters, emulsify each. Safe for learners.
Phaco chop (horizontal/vertical): faster, less energy. Stop and chop = hybrid.
Cortex: aspirate, peel to the centre (I/A, bimanual, Simcoe).
IOL: fill the bag with cohesive OVD, inject and unfold. Rotate toric to axis. Remove OVD.
Finish: hydroseal wounds, intracameral antibiotic (e.g. cefuroxime) ± subconj.
Femtosecond laser: automates incisions, capsulotomy, nuclear fragmentation, LRIs. Precise, but costly and slower.
chunks.hook: Phaco recipe: Clean → Cut → Circle (rhexis) → Float (hydro) → Crack → Clean up → Lens in.

cards.q: Minimum contact time for povidone-iodine before surgery?
Purpose of hydrodissection?
cards.a: Separate the nucleus/cortex from the capsule so it can rotate and be removed.

chunks.title: Posterior capsule rupture & dropped lens
chunks.tldr: PC rupture: AC suddenly deepens/shallows, pupil briefly dilates. Plug with dispersive OVD, lower flow, clear vitreous (triamcinolone to see it), 3-piece IOL in the sulcus (optic capture if possible).
points: Other signs: nucleus falls away, aspiration slows (vitreous in the tip), visible tear/vitreous.
Vitreous loss sequelae: CMO, RD, endophthalmitis, peaked pupil, vitreous wick, glaucoma, IOL dislocation.
Manage: dispersive OVD, convert to ECCE if a big nucleus remains, Sheets glide, low bottle/flow phaco, dry cortex aspiration.
Bimanual anterior vitrectomy (infusion high, cutter low). Triamcinolone or trypan to see vitreous.
IOL: small tear → in the bag. Big tear → 3-piece in the sulcus, optic capture through the rhexis (same power or −0.5 D; without capture −0.5 to −1.0 D).
No support → AC IOL + peripheral iridectomy (risk: bullous keratopathy, hyphaema) or iris/scleral-fixated lens.
Suture the wound after any PC rupture. Acetylcholine to constrict the pupil.
Dropped lens fragments: glaucoma, uveitis, RD, CMO → treat IOP/inflammation → PPV for big pieces.
Dropped IOL/bag (e.g. PXF): PPV with reposition/exchange.
chunks.hook: Capsule breaks: Stop, Plug (dispersive), Slow down, Sweep vitreous, Sulcus lens.

cards.q: What helps visualise vitreous strands in the AC during vitrectomy?
AC IOL inserted: what extra step is mandatory?

chunks.title: Suprachoroidal haemorrhage
chunks.tldr: AC suddenly shallows, IOP rises, iris prolapses, dark mound behind the pupil → close the wound NOW (suture). Drain later (7–14 days) if needed.
points: Bleed from a posterior ciliary artery into the suprachoroidal space. Severe = expulsive.
Risks: old age, glaucoma, long eye, cardiovascular disease, vitreous loss, conversion to ECCE.
Signs: shallowing AC, high IOP, iris prolapse, vitreous extrusion, loss of red reflex, dark mound.
Act: suture shut immediately (leave the OVD). No posterior sclerostomy during surgery.
After: acetazolamide, intensive steroids, antibiotics, avoid NSAIDs, pause anticoagulants if safe.
Drain at 7–14 days once the clot liquefies. Retinal apposition >14 days ('kissing') → worse prognosis. PPV if RD.
chunks.hook: Dark mound rising → shut the door (suture).

cards.q: First action for intraoperative suprachoroidal haemorrhage?
cards.a: Immediately close the wound with sutures.

cards.q: When is drainage of a suprachoroidal haemorrhage usually performed?
cards.a: 7–14 days later, once the clot has liquefied.

chunks.title: Acute endophthalmitis: recognise & prevent
chunks.tldr: Days after surgery: pain, red eye, vision drop, hypopyon, vitritis. Mostly Staph epidermidis (90% Gram-positive). Prevent with povidone-iodine 5% + intracameral cefuroxime.
points: Incidence ~0.1%. Toxins + inflammation destroy photoreceptors fast.
Risks: PC rupture, long surgery, combined procedures, clear corneal sutureless/temporal wound, leaking wound day 1, topical anaesthesia, lid disease, diabetes.
Source: patient's own lid/conjunctival flora.

Prevent: povidone-iodine 5% ≥3 min, drape lashes, treat blepharitis/dacryocystitis/other socket first, intracameral cefuroxime 1 mg/0.1 ml (or moxifloxacin). Avoid intracameral vancomycin (HORV). Resuture leaks.
Signs: lid swelling, chemosis, RAPD, corneal haze, fibrin, hypopyon, vitritis, poor red reflex.
Differentials: retained lens matter, vitreous haemorrhage, sterile uveitis (trial of steroid, review in 6–24 h), TASS (toxic reaction to fluids: fibrin + corneal oedema within a day, no infection).
If in doubt, treat as infection.
chunks.hook: Painful red eye + hypopyon after cataract surgery = endophthalmitis until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Most common organism in acute post-cataract endophthalmitis?
Why avoid routine intracameral vancomycin?
cards.a: Risk of haemorrhagic occlusive retinal vasculitis (HORV).

chunks.title: Acute endophthalmitis: tap & inject
chunks.tldr: Tap (aqueous + vitreous) and inject: intravitreal vancomycin 2 mg + ceftazidime 2 mg (amikacin 0.4 mg if penicillin-allergic). EVS: vision PL only → immediate vitrectomy.
points: No view → B-scan first (exclude RD).
Aqueous: 0.1–0.2 ml via paracentesis (25 G). Vitreous: 0.2–0.4 ml, 3.5 mm behind the limbus (pseudophakic), needle or vitrector. Vitreous is more often positive.
Send immediately (microscopy, culture, PCR).
Intravitreal: vancomycin 2 mg/0.1 ml (Gram+ incl. MRSA) + ceftazidime 2 mg/0.1 ml (Gram−, Pseudomonas). Amikacin 0.4 mg if allergic (more retinal toxicity).
Plus: oral moxifloxacin 400 mg ×10 days, topical antibiotics, topical dexamethasone, atropine.
Oral pred 1 mg/kg after 12–24 h in severe cases (if fungus excluded).
Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study: VA light perception → immediate PPV (halves severe vision loss). HM or better → tap and inject.
Worse at 48 h → review sensitivities, PPV, repeat injection.
Outcome: PL at presentation → 30% reach 6/12. Better than PL → 60%. Bacillus cereus, Strep → poor.
chunks.hook: Light perception only? Vitrectomy. Better than that? Tap and inject.

cards.q: Standard intravitreal antibiotics for endophthalmitis?
cards.a: Vancomycin 2 mg/0.1 ml + ceftazidime 2 mg/0.1 ml.

cards.q: EVS criterion for immediate vitrectomy?
cards.a: Presenting VA of light perception only.

chunks.title: Delayed (chronic) endophthalmitis
chunks.tldr: Months after surgery: painless, low-grade uveitis with big KPs and a white capsular plaque that keeps relapsing when steroids stop → P. acnes.
points: Low-virulence bug (Propionibacterium/Cutibacterium acnes) trapped in the capsular bag, hiding in macrophages.
Onset 4 weeks to years (average 9 months). Can be triggered by YAG capsulotomy.
Signs: mild AC inflammation, medium-large KPs, vitritis, white capsular plaque.
Responds to steroids, then relapses → eventually steroid-resistant.
First try: oral moxifloxacin (or clarithromycin) 10–14 days.
Then: aqueous/vitreous tap, anaerobic culture (10–14 days), PCR.
Definitive: PPV + remove capsular bag/IOL + intravitreal vancomycin. Injection alone usually fails.
chunks.hook: Plaque in the bag = P. acnes.

cards.q: Organism in chronic saccular endophthalmitis?
Definitive treatment?
cards.a: Vitrectomy with capsular bag (± IOL) removal and intravitreal vancomycin.

chunks.title: PCO & YAG capsulotomy
chunks.tldr: PCO = commonest late complication (20–25%): blur, glare. Elschnig pearls or fibrosis. Fix with Nd:YAG capsulotomy (~4–5 mm, start 1 mJ).
points: Leftover lens epithelial cells grow on the back capsule.
Less PCO: rhexis overlapping the optic, square-edged IOL. More PCO: PMMA, hydrogel.
Pearl type (Elschnig pearls, swollen cells) and fibrosis type. Soemmering ring = doughnut of cells in the bag periphery.
YAG: start 1 mJ, cruciate or circular, opening ≈ scotopic pupil (~4–5 mm), don't go past the optic edge. Keep total energy low (<80 mJ).
Be cautious in: high myopes (RD), uveitis (CMO), PXF (lens dislocation).
Complications: IOL pitting, IOP spike, RD (warn myopes about flashes/floaters), CMO (less if after 6 months), IOL shift.
Capsulophimosis: rhexis shrinks (small rhexis, PXF, RP, plate silicone IOL) → YAG anterior relaxing cuts.
chunks.hook: YAG = 'Yes, Again Good vision'. Warn myopes about RD.

cards.q: Most common late complication of cataract surgery?
Name 2 risk factors for anterior capsular phimosis.
cards.a: Pseudoexfoliation, small capsulorhexis (also RP, plate silicone IOL).

chunks.title: CMO, dysphotopsia & other late problems
chunks.tldr: Irvine–Gass CMO peaks 6–10 weeks: blurry near vision → OCT → topical NSAID ± steroid. Negative dysphotopsia = dark temporal crescent.
points: CMO risks: ERM, CMO in the other eye, vitreous loss/wick, AC IOL, secondary IOL, prostaglandin drops, diabetes, uveitis.
CMO treatment: NSAID drops (ketorolac, bromfenac, nepafenac) for months, steroids (topical, periocular, intravitreal), CAIs, anti-VEGF, YAG/vitrectomy for vitreous wick, PPV.

Dysphotopsia (~1 in 10): negative = dark temporal shadow (most bothersome). Positive = streaks, haloes, flashes. Usually improves. Options: reverse optic capture, sulcus IOL/piggyback, IOL exchange. Avoid YAG (makes exchange hard).
Ptosis: wait a year.
IOL malposition: reposition or exchange.
Corneal decompensation: low cell count, dense nucleus, long surgery, PXF, high IOP → dispersive OVD protection.
RD: lattice, breaks, high myopia, vitreous loss. Usually PPV.

Refractive surprise: refract, check for CMO (hyperopic) or capsular block (myopic), recheck biometry/K (missed keratoconus, prior LASIK). Fix: glasses/CL, early IOL exchange, laser refractive surgery, piggyback.
chunks.hook: CMO after cataract = 2 months later, can't read → NSAID drops.

cards.q: Peak onset of pseudophakic CMO?
Dark temporal crescent after uncomplicated phaco?

chunks.title: Causes of congenital cataract
chunks.tldr: ~3 per 10,000 births. Bilateral → often AD inherited, also metabolic, infection, chromosomal. Unilateral → usually sporadic, healthy baby. Oil droplet = galactosaemia.
points: Galactosaemia (AR, GPUT deficiency): oil-droplet cataract in weeks. Remove milk → can reverse. Otherwise fatal.
Lowe syndrome (X-linked, OCRL1): cataract always, microphakia, congenital glaucoma (~50%), kidney problems. Carriers have lens dots.
Mannosidosis: spoke-like posterior cortical dots. Also Fabry, hypoparathyroidism, glucose problems.
Infections (TORCH): rubella (pearly nuclear cataract ~15%), toxo, CMV, varicella, measles, syphilis, HSV, HIV.
Down syndrome (75% cataract, late childhood), Brushfield spots, keratoconus. Edwards (trisomy 18).
Hallermann–Streiff (90%), Nance–Horan (X-linked, carriers have Y-suture opacities).
Morphology: blue dot (harmless), nuclear, coronary, lamellar with riders, oil droplet, sutural, anterior polar, posterior polar (capsule may be missing → ruptures in surgery).
chunks.hook: Galactose = oil drop. Stop the milk!

cards.q: 'Oil droplet' cataract in a neonate?
Congenital cataract + glaucoma + renal tubular problems in a boy?
Which congenital cataract has a high risk of capsule rupture during surgery?

chunks.title: Managing congenital cataract
chunks.tldr: Dense bilateral → operate at 4–10 weeks. Dense unilateral → by 6 weeks + aggressive patching. Too early (<4 weeks) → more glaucoma. Always do posterior capsulorhexis + vitrectomy.
points: Significance: no red reflex = dense. Can see vessels with indirect but not direct = significant (>3 mm central/posterior). Nystagmus, no fixation, squint = bad signs.
Check family members. B-scan if no view (PFV?). VEP, preferential looking.
Investigations (non-familial): TORCH, urine reducing substances (galactosaemia), amino acids (Lowe), glucose, calcium, phosphate, GPUT.
Bilateral dense: surgery 4–10 weeks, worse eye first.
Unilateral dense: 4–6 weeks, then hard patching. Found after 16 weeks → poor prognosis.
Partial: observe, dilate, part-time patch.
Surgery: rhexis, aspirate, posterior capsulorhexis + anterior vitrectomy, ± IOL.
Complications: PCO (almost certain if capsule left), membranes, Soemmering ring, glaucoma (up to 20% by 5 years; earlier surgery = more), pupil block (microphthalmos), RD.
Rehab: contact lenses (best for aphakia), glasses (bilateral), IOL (aim hyperopic; myopic shift with growth). Treat amblyopia.
chunks.hook: Earlier = less amblyopia, more glaucoma. Sweet spot ~4–6 weeks.

cards.q: Why avoid operating on congenital cataract before ~4 weeks?
cards.a: Higher risk of later aphakic/secondary glaucoma.

cards.q: Latest recommended time for surgery on a dense unilateral congenital cataract?

chunks.title: Displaced lens: which way & why
chunks.tldr: Marfan → lens goes UP and out (superotemporal), zonules intact. Homocystinuria → DOWN and in (inferonasal), zonules dissolve. Weill–Marchesani → small round lens → pupil block.
points: Subluxated (still in the pupil) vs luxated (fully out). Phacodonesis = wobbly lens.
Acquired: trauma (commonest), PXF, chronic uveitis, syphilis, hypermature cataract, buphthalmos/high myopia, ciliary body tumour.
Familial ectopia lentis (AD): both eyes, superotemporal.
Ectopia lentis et pupillae (AR): lens and pupil go opposite directions, small pupils.
Marfan (AD, FBN1): tall, long limbs/fingers, high palate, aortic root dilatation/dissection, mitral prolapse. Lens superotemporal (80%), accommodation kept. Also glaucoma, lattice → RD.
Weill–Marchesani (AR/AD FBN1): short, stubby fingers. Microspherophakia → lens falls inferiorly / into the AC → pupil block angle closure.
Homocystinuria (AR): blond hair, blue eyes, malar flush, Marfanoid, learning delay, thrombosis (GA risk!). Lens inferonasal, zonules (cysteine-poor) break down. Treat with B6, folate, B12.
Others: sulfite oxidase deficiency (always), Stickler, Ehlers–Danlos, hyperlysinaemia.
Manage: glasses/aphakic correction. Surgery for intractable refraction, amblyopia, cataract, glaucoma, uveitis, corneal touch.
chunks.hook: Marfan looks UP (tall people look up). Homocystinuria goes DOWN (homes are on the ground).

cards.q: Typical direction of lens subluxation in Marfan syndrome?
Inferonasal subluxation + thromboembolic risk?
Short stature + brachydactyly + microspherophakia + angle closure?

chunks.title: Lenticonus, microspherophakia, coloboma
chunks.tldr: Anterior lenticonus = Alport (deaf + kidneys). Posterior lenticonus = one eye, sporadic. Lens 'coloboma' = zonular gap, not a true coloboma.
points: Anterior lenticonus: both eyes, front of the lens bulges forward, oil-droplet reflex. Almost always Alport syndrome (sensorineural deafness, nephritis). Also retinal flecks, PPCD.
Posterior lenticonus: back bulges, thin/absent capsule. Usually one eye, sporadic. PSC develops, can suddenly opacify.
Lentiglobus: whole lens hemispherical (rare).
Microspherophakia: small round lens. Weill–Marchesani, Marfan, hyperlysinaemia, rubella, Peters. → lenticular myopia, subluxation, pupil block.
Microphakia: small diameter (Lowe).
Lens coloboma: notch in the edge from missing zonules.
chunks.hook: Anterior lenticonus = Alport.

cards.q: Anterior lenticonus is associated with?
What actually causes a 'lens coloboma'?
cards.a: Localised zonular deficiency (not a true coloboma).
